quiz.q: Which macro returns a String instead of printing anything?
quiz.explain: format! builds and returns a String; the print macros write directly to stdout or stderr.

quiz.q: What's the difference between `{}` and `{:?}` in a format string?
quiz.explain: {} calls the Display trait (user-facing text); {:?} calls Debug (developer-facing, usually derived).

quiz.q: Why does `{p:?}` fail to compile if `Point` has no `#[derive(Debug)]`?
options: It doesn't fail — it just prints nothing
{:?} requires the Debug trait, which the compiler checks at compile time
quiz.explain: {:?} is a real trait bound (Debug). Without an implementation the code fails to compile — it never silently prints blank.
`03` means zero-padded to a minimum width of 3, giving "007".

quiz.q: What does precision (`.N`) mean when applied to a string argument, e.g. `{s:.5}`?
options: Truncate the string to at most 5 characters
quiz.explain: For strings, precision means "maximum length" — the string is truncated to that many characters.

options: Field access isn't allowed anywhere in println!
Captured identifiers in format strings must be plain variable names, not expressions like field access
quiz.explain: Implicit argument capture only works for a bare identifier already in scope; field access must be passed as a normal argument, e.g. `println!("{}", p.score)`.

quiz.q: What must you do with the Result returned by `write!(buf, "...")`?
options: Handle it (e.g. .unwrap() or ?) — Rust warns on an unused Result
Only handle it when writing to a file, not a String
quiz.explain: write!/writeln! return a Result because the write can fail; leaving it unhandled triggers an "unused Result that must be used" warning.

quiz.q: When are format string arguments (like `{name}` or `{0}`) checked for correctness?
options: At runtime, the first time the line executes
At compile time, as part of expanding the macro
Never — invalid references are silently ignored
quiz.explain: format!/println! expand and validate the format string at compile time, so a typo or missing argument is a build error, not a runtime surprise.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between println! and format!?
flashcards.back: println! prints to stdout with a trailing newline; format! builds and returns a String without printing.

flashcards.front: Which macro prints to stderr instead of stdout?
flashcards.back: eprintln! (and eprint! without the trailing newline).

flashcards.front: What trait does {} use? What about {:?}?
flashcards.back: {} uses Display (user-facing); {:?} uses Debug (developer-facing, usually derived).
It pretty-prints the Debug output across multiple indented lines instead of one line.

flashcards.front: What does the format spec `{value:>8.2}` mean?
flashcards.back: Right-align (>), minimum width 8, 2 digits of precision (decimal places for a float).

flashcards.front: Can you capture a field access like {player.score} directly in a format string?
flashcards.back: No — only plain variable names can be captured; expressions must be passed as a regular argument.

flashcards.front: What's required to implement Display for a custom type?
flashcards.back: `impl fmt::Display for T { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result { write!(f, ...) } }`

flashcards.front: When are format string errors caught?
flashcards.back: At compile time — invalid syntax or a missing argument fails the build.
